text.p: Learning from the best in the world would help Europe's governments boost industry competitiveness and catch up with the United States and Japan, leading European industrialists said on Friday.
"Competitiveness is a major problem for Europe," said Daniel Jansson, chairman of Belgian chemical group Solvay.
At the moment, Janssen told a news conference, Europe was "not winning the race, but we are losing the race."
He was presenting a report by the European Round Table of Industrialists (ERT) on using so called benchmarking as a tool to improve Europe's competitive power, growth and job creation.
"Benchmarking is looking at 'the best in the class', learning from this experience and then trying to do as well or better," the report said.
The ERT groups 46 chairmen of major European companies, ranging from Italian carmaker Fiat to Swedish telecommunications group Ericsson and Finnish forestry giant UPM-Kymmene.
Benchmarking has been used for some time with success by companies such as oil giant British Petroleum but also by the Australian and Dutch governments, he said.

"It can reveal the positive achievements of very different countries, in policy areas where it may be countries as far away as Chile or Singapore that have become the world's pace setter," the report said.
"It can help to achieve results where results are desperately needed, above all in the overwhelming battle against unemployment in Europe," it added.

Between 1973 and 1994, the United States created 34 million new private sector jobs and Japan 11 million new jobs but the European Union no new jobs -- figures which highlight Europe's disappointing jobs record in recent decades.
Benchmarking in public policy could help improve the situation, Janssen said, by changing attitudes, policies and regulations to increase Europe's competitiveness.
The report said BP from a poor starting point had been able to achieve a steady improvement against its main competitors by using benchmarking to target cost reductions.

The Australian government had used it to improve its infrastructure, especially its port facilities, while the tool prompted the Dutch government to simplify regulations and to open markets for new entrepreneurs.
At EU level, meeting the single currency criteria is a form of benchmarking, Janssen said.
He said it could be used to help boost the competitiveness of costly services crucial for industry, such as telecommunications, energy and transportation.
It could also help the situation for innovation and tecnology development as well as for labour markets, including labour costs, flexibility and minimum wages.
"We urge governments to maximise the potential for comparisons with the best," the report said.

The report -- "Benchmarking for policy-makers -- the way to competitiveness, growth and job creation" -- was published at a time when the principle of benchmarking seems to be gaining ground in the EU.

Last week, the Commission proposed in a Communication benchmarking as a tool for the enhancement of EU competitiveness and the Irish presidency plans to propose a Council resolution on bechmarking to the Industry Council on November 14.
